newsitem.title: SPAIN: Latam needs major reforms to lock in recovery - IADB.
newsitem.headline: Latam needs major reforms to lock in recovery - IADB.

text.p: Latin America has emerged from recession far faster than hoped but it still needs major reforms to lock in its recovery, the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) said on Monday.

While Latin America and the Caribbean recorded growth of more than three percent in 1996, well above the 1995 crisis level of less than one percent, improvements in savings and investment were imperative to ensure that regional growth was maintained, the IADB said in its yearly report, released at its 38th annual meeting in Barcelona.
"The challenge that the region now faces is to transform the recovery into sustained and shared growth," the bank said.
"Rates of investment and saving remain insufficient in most countries to sustain adequate rates of growth in output and employment opportunities."

Latin America was plunged into economic and financial crisis in 1995 after Mexico sharply devalued the peso. But the bank said recovery there and in Argentina, the two nations hardest hit by recession, was well under way and international confidence had been restored.
But the modest increase in growth across most of the region was matched by what preliminary figures show is a rise in unemployment.
"Unemployment remains stubbornly high, highlighting the urgent need to reassess labour market regulations," it said.
IADB President Enrique Iglesias said in a interview published on Saturday that Latin America should aim to clock up double last year's growth rate.
"To have the whole population benefit from growth we should double the rate of 3.5 percent averaged between 1990 and 1994," he said.

On the positive side, inflation has fallen to its lowest in almost two decades, private capital inflows have recovered nearly to pre-crisis levels, and nations like Argentina, Colombia and Mexico have been able to lengthen the maturity of their international debt issues, reducing their vulnerability to future crises.
"The median rate of inflation fell to 11 percent in 1996 compared with 13 percent in 1995 and was the lowest rate since 1977," the report said.
Exports from the region rose about 13 percent, and real investment grew by nearly six percent last year.
Net capital flows to the region totalled about $60 billion, the private capital proportion rebounding to their peak 1992-94 levels.
But the bank stressed that the region must press on with both economic and social reform so the benefits of the revival can be more equitably shared.

"This will require more investments, in both quantity and quality, in education and health,...a reassessment of labour market regulations and their impact on the overall economy, reform of public pension systems, and consolidation of the fiscal reforms already undertaken," it said.
The IADB was the leading source of multilateral lending to Latin America and the Caribbean in 1996 for the third consecutive year, approving $6.76 billion in loans and disbursing $4.37 billion.
Approximately a third of its loans are targeted at projects that will help raise the standard of living and alleviate poverty in the region.

Projects it supported last year included direct finance for a Guatemalan plan consolidating national reconciliation after its recent guerrilla war, and the approval of financing for social security and pension reform in Argentina, Mexico and Uruguay.
